locator.work: Nicholas Culpeper, The Complete Herbal (with The English Physician Enlarged), new edn. 1850 — Project Gutenberg eBook #49513, public domain
locator.heading: Endive

source_text:
_Descript._] COMMON garden Endive bears a longer and larger leaf than
Succory, and abides but one year, quickly running up to a stalk and
seed, and then perishes; it has blue flowers, and the seed of the
ordinary Endive is so like Succory seed, that it is hard to distinguish
them.

_Government and virtues._] It is a fine cooling, cleansing, jovial
plant. The decoction of the leaves, or the juice, or the distilled
water of Endive, serve well to cool the excessive heat of the liver
and stomach, and in the hot fits of agues, and all other inflammations
in any part of the body; it cools the heat and sharpness of the
urine, and excoriation in the urinary parts. The seeds are of the
same property, or rather more powerful, and besides are available for
fainting, swoonings, and passions of the heart. Outwardly applied, they
serve to temper the sharp humours of fretting ulcers, hot tumours,
swellings, and pestilential sores; and wonderfully help not only the
redness and inflammations of the eyes, but the dimness of the sight
also; they are also used to allay the pains of the gout. You cannot use
it amiss; a syrup of it is a fine cooling medicine for fevers.

evidence.summary: Modern evidence links Cichorium endivia to skin inflammation management and organ protection. Chemical profiling identifies phenolic acids as key constituents. Direct clinical validation for historical uses like urinary sharpness or fainting is absent in current literature.

concordance.rationale: Modern evidence (PMID:12793186, 36009533) offers limited preclinical data on phenolics and testicular protection. No clinical trials support historical claims for liver cooling, agues, or urinary excoriation.
concordance.uncertainty: High due to lack of human clinical trials matching specific historical indications like 'hot fits' or 'sharpness of urine'.
caveats: No safety data for chronic use.

issues: Grade 'C' is unearned: The entry lacks EMA approval (confirmed false) and PubMed evidence count is only 3. The rationale cites specific modern preclinical studies but fails to provide the actual text quotes or concordance data required to substantiate even a partial grade without clinical trials. In strict auditing, a grade of 'C' implies some validated efficacy; with only 3 preclinical papers and no clinical trials for the specific historical indications, the evidence base is insufficient to justify any positive concordance grade beyond 'D' or 'E' (insufficient/contradictory). The entry admits 'partial' support based on limited preclinical data which contradicts the strict requirement that the graph only admits audited entries with robust evidence. Additionally, the 'source' for taxon resolution is 'LLM_knowledge' without external citation, violating completeness rules for scientific names.
